summary: Looks at what happens when IPv6 hosts keep using stale prefixes after a network renumbers without warning, for example when a router reboots and forgets its old prefixes. It describes the problem and recommends improvements, so hosts do not go on using bad addresses for a long time.

eli5.summary: If your street gets renamed without telling anyone, mail still goes to the old name. This explains how computers can notice sooner and switch.

questions: ipv6 stale prefix after router reboot
what is flash renumbering in ipv6
why do ipv6 addresses stay valid so long
how to fix ipv6 prefix changes
subtitle: How IPv6 hosts can handle sudden prefix changes when routers lose their memory.

tldr.problem: When a router suddenly changes IPv6 prefixes without warning (for example after rebooting), hosts keep using old addresses for days or weeks, causing connectivity failures. This happens because the default lifetime values for prefix information are very long.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes why this happens and recommends operational mitigations: using stable prefixes when possible, or reducing the lifetime values routers advertise so hosts deprecate stale addresses faster.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can improve resilience to flash-renumbering events by adjusting SLAAC parameters. Future work aims to improve both routers and hosts to detect and react to these events.

today: RFC 8978 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted. It describes an operational problem and recommends mitigations that networks can implement today while waiting for protocol improvements in SLAAC.

sections.title: Flash-Renumbering Events
sections.content:
IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) allows hosts to automatically configure addresses by listening to Router Advertisement (RA) messages. These messages include Prefix Information Options (PIOs) that tell hosts which prefixes to use and how long they are valid.

Normally, IPv6 assumes prefixes are stable. But in some scenarios, a prefix can suddenly become invalid without warning: a router crashes and reboots with a different prefix, a configuration system pushes a new prefix without notifying hosts, or a network gets renumbered by mistake. This is called a flash-renumbering event. When it happens without explicit signaling, hosts continue using stale (no longer valid) addresses for an unacceptably long time.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a router suddenly gets a new network prefix without telling anyone. Hosts don't realize the old prefix is bad, so they keep using it.

sections.title: Why the Problem Occurs
sections.content:
Three main factors make flash-renumbering events problematic. First, many IPv6 deployments use dynamic prefixes: ISPs assign temporary prefixes that change on each connection. A 2018 survey found 37% of responding ISPs use dynamic IPv6 prefixes.

Second, the default lifetimes in RFC 4861 are very long: addresses stay preferred for 7 days and remain valid for 30 days. If a prefix becomes stale without explicit signaling, hosts may actively use bad addresses for a full week before even deprecating them.

Third, SLAAC hosts cannot easily recover from stale information. Even if a router tries to explicitly invalidate a prefix (by sending an RA with zero lifetimes), RFC 4862 limits the minimum valid lifetime to 2 hours in unauthenticated RAs to prevent malicious downgrade attacks. This means hosts cannot be forced to immediately forget a stale prefix.
sections.eli5: Routers keep prefixes valid for 30 days by default. If a prefix becomes bad without a warning, computers keep using it for weeks. Even if the router tries to say 'this prefix is bad,' the computers ignore extreme changes for safety.

sections.title: Operational Mitigations
sections.content:
While permanent solutions require updates to SLAAC itself, network operators can reduce the problem today through two main approaches.

Stable prefixes: If an ISP assigns stable IPv6 prefixes that never change (even across router reboots), flash-renumbering events simply do not occur. However, this is not always feasible: some provisioning systems cannot deliver stable prefixes, and stable prefixes have privacy implications and routing complexity.

SLAAC parameter tweaking: Operators can reduce the advertised lifetimes from the RFC 4861 defaults to values like 45 minutes (Preferred Lifetime) and 90 minutes (Valid Lifetime). Shorter lifetimes mean stale addresses are deprecated and invalidated more quickly, reducing the window of broken connectivity. Under normal operation with regular Router Advertisements refreshing the lifetimes, this adjustment has no impact. But if a router fails to send updates (the flash-renumbering scenario), hosts recover in minutes rather than weeks.

When using DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation, a router advertising sub-prefixes must ensure the SLAAC lifetimes do not extend past the DHCPv6 lease time.
sections.eli5: Networks can either give out prefixes that never change, or make prefixes expire quickly so stale ones stop being used sooner.

sections.title: Future Improvements
sections.content:
This document identifies areas where SLAAC and IPv6 protocols themselves can be improved. Ongoing work includes:

Router improvements: Customer Edge routers should be able to detect and signal stale prefixes even when they have no memory of previously advertised prefixes. One approach is to deprecate any prefix from which the router receives packets that do not match currently advertised prefixes.

Host improvements: Hosts could be enhanced to recover from stale configuration information more quickly, for example by using lower default lifetimes or implementing smarter address selection that avoids stale prefixes. Some work in this area is happening in the IETF 6man working group.

These improvements are necessary for robustness because, as this document notes, flash-renumbering events will continue to happen in the real world despite operator best efforts.
sections.eli5: Future routers and computers may get better at noticing when a prefix has gone bad and switching to a new one automatically.
